title: English Usually Needs a Subject
html:
Chapter 1

English Usually Needs a Subject

Sentence Foundations
Big Idea

English usually needs a visible subject.

Simple Rule

English sentence pattern: subject + verb.

Spanish Comparison

Spanish often allows the subject to disappear because the verb ending gives enough information.

Contrast box

Spanish thinkingNatural English
Hablo inglés.I speak English.
Common Mistake
IncorrectCorrect
Speak English.I speak English.
Why This Happens

This mistake makes sense. Spanish and English organize this idea differently. The goal is not to think “Spanish is wrong,” but to notice where Spanish patterns can interfere with English sentence-building. Once you see the pattern, you can practice the English structure as a whole phrase.

Real English Examples
  • I work every day.
  • She lives in Florida.
  • They study English.
  • It is raining.
  • We have class today.
  • You speak Spanish.
  • He needs help.
  • The teacher explains the lesson.
Practice
  1. Fix the mistake: Speak English.
  2. Translate into English: Hablo inglés
  3. Build your own sentence using the rule from this chapter.
  4. Choose the correct answer: I speak English. / Speak English.
Show answers
  1. I speak English.
  2. Answers may vary, but they should follow the chapter pattern.
  3. Answers may vary.
  4. Choose: I speak English.
Teacher / Academic Note

This chapter addresses subject omission, a common area where Spanish-speaking learners may transfer patterns from Spanish into English. In second language learning, this kind of predictable transfer can be reduced through noticing, contrastive examples, repeated input, and deliberate practice (Swan, 2016; Swan & Smith, 2001).

Quick Review
  • Learn the English pattern as a whole structure.
  • Do not translate word-for-word from Spanish.
  • Practice with short, correct sentences before building longer ones.
  • Use the examples in this chapter as sentence models.
Sources and Further Reading
  • Swan, 2016; Swan & Smith, 2001

Chapter 1

English Usually Needs a Subject

Sentence Foundations
Big Idea

El inglés normalmente necesita un sujeto visible.

Simple Rule

Patrón de oración inglesa: sujeto + verbo.

Spanish Comparison

En español, el sujeto puede desaparecer porque la terminación del verbo da suficiente información.

Caja de contraste

Pensamiento en españolInglés natural
Hablo inglés.I speak English.
Common Mistake
IncorrectoCorrecto
Speak English.I speak English.
Why This Happens

Este error tiene sentido. El español y el inglés organizan esta idea de forma diferente. La meta no es pensar que "el español está mal", sino notar dónde los patrones del español pueden interferir con la construcción de oraciones en inglés. Cuando ves el patrón, puedes practicar la estructura inglesa como una frase completa.

Real English Examples
  • I work every day.
  • She lives in Florida.
  • They study English.
  • It is raining.
  • We have class today.
  • You speak Spanish.
  • He needs help.
  • The teacher explains the lesson.
Practice
  1. Corrige el error: Speak English.
  2. Traduce al inglés: Hablo inglés
  3. Construye tu propia oración usando la regla de este capítulo.
  4. Elige la respuesta correcta: I speak English. / Speak English.
Show answers
  1. I speak English.
  2. Las respuestas pueden variar, pero deben seguir el patrón del capítulo.
  3. Las respuestas pueden variar.
  4. Elige: I speak English.
Teacher / Academic Note

Este capítulo trata sobre omisión del sujeto, una zona común donde los aprendices hispanohablantes pueden transferir patrones del español al inglés. En el aprendizaje de segundas lenguas, este tipo de transferencia previsible se reduce notando los patrones, comparando ejemplos contrastivos, recibiendo entrada repetida y haciendo práctica deliberada (Swan, 2016; Swan & Smith, 2001).

Quick Review
  • Aprende el patrón inglés como una estructura completa.
  • No traduzcas palabra por palabra desde el español.
  • Practica con oraciones cortas y correctas antes de hacer oraciones largas.
  • Usa los ejemplos de este capítulo como modelos de oración.
Sources and Further Reading
  • Swan, 2016; Swan & Smith, 2001
html_fr:
Chapter 1

English Usually Needs a Subject

Sentence Foundations
Big Idea

L'anglais a généralement besoin d'un sujet visible.

Simple Rule

Schéma de la phrase anglaise : sujet + verbe.

Spanish Comparison

L'espagnol permet souvent au sujet de disparaître parce que la terminaison du verbe donne assez d'information.

Encadré de contraste

Pensée espagnoleAnglais naturel
Hablo inglés.I speak English.
Common Mistake
IncorrectCorrect
Speak English.I speak English.
Why This Happens

Cette erreur se comprend. L'espagnol et l'anglais organisent cette idée différemment. L'objectif n'est pas de penser que « l'espagnol se trompe », mais de remarquer où les schémas espagnols peuvent interférer avec la construction de phrases en anglais. Une fois le schéma identifié, on peut pratiquer la structure anglaise comme une expression complète.

Real English Examples
  • I work every day.
  • She lives in Florida.
  • They study English.
  • It is raining.
  • We have class today.
  • You speak Spanish.
  • He needs help.
  • The teacher explains the lesson.
Practice
  1. Corrigez l'erreur : Speak English.
  2. Traduisez en anglais : Hablo inglés
  3. Construisez votre propre phrase en utilisant la règle de ce chapitre.
  4. Choisissez la bonne réponse : I speak English. / Speak English.
Show answers
  1. I speak English.
  2. Les réponses peuvent varier, mais elles doivent suivre le schéma du chapitre.
  3. Les réponses peuvent varier.
  4. Choisissez : I speak English.
Teacher / Academic Note

Ce chapitre traite de omission du sujet, un domaine fréquent où les apprenants hispanophones peuvent transférer des schémas de l'espagnol vers l'anglais. En acquisition d'une seconde langue, ce type de transfert prévisible se réduit par la prise de conscience, les exemples contrastifs, l'exposition répétée et la pratique délibérée (Swan, 2016; Swan & Smith, 2001).

Quick Review
  • Apprenez le schéma anglais comme une structure complète.
  • Ne traduisez pas mot à mot depuis l'espagnol.
  • Pratiquez avec des phrases courtes et correctes avant d'en construire de plus longues.
  • Servez-vous des exemples de ce chapitre comme modèles de phrase.
Sources and Further Reading
  • Swan, 2016; Swan & Smith, 2001

title: Basic English Word Order
html:
Chapter 2

Basic English Word Order

Sentence Foundations
Big Idea

English word order is less flexible than Spanish word order.

Simple Rule

Use Subject + Verb + Object for basic sentences.

Spanish Comparison

Spanish can move words around more easily for emphasis. English usually cannot.

Contrast box

Spanish thinkingNatural English
Como pizza.I eat pizza.
Common Mistake
IncorrectCorrect
Pizza eat I.I eat pizza.
Why This Happens

This mistake makes sense. Spanish and English organize this idea differently. The goal is not to think “Spanish is wrong,” but to notice where Spanish patterns can interfere with English sentence-building. Once you see the pattern, you can practice the English structure as a whole phrase.

Real English Examples
  • I drink coffee.
  • She reads books.
  • We watch movies.
  • They play soccer.
  • He studies English.
  • I like music.
  • She buys food.
  • We visit friends.
Practice
  1. Fix the mistake: Pizza eat I.
  2. Translate into English: Como pizza
  3. Build your own sentence using the rule from this chapter.
  4. Choose the correct answer: I eat pizza. / Pizza eat I.
Show answers
  1. I eat pizza.
  2. Answers may vary, but they should follow the chapter pattern.
  3. Answers may vary.
  4. Choose: I eat pizza.
Teacher / Academic Note

This chapter addresses SVO word order, a common area where Spanish-speaking learners may transfer patterns from Spanish into English. In second language learning, this kind of predictable transfer can be reduced through noticing, contrastive examples, repeated input, and deliberate practice (Biber et al., 1999).

Quick Review

  • Do not translate word-for-word from Spanish.
  • Practice with short, correct sentences before building longer ones.
  • Use the examples in this chapter as sentence models.
Sources and Further Reading

title: Questions with Do, Does, and Did

Chapter 3

Questions with Do, Does, and Did

Sentence Foundations
Big Idea

English often uses do, does, and did to make questions.

Simple Rule

Use Do/Does/Did + subject + base verb.

Spanish Comparison

Spanish can form questions with intonation. English usually needs a helper verb.

Contrast box

Spanish thinkingNatural English
¿Trabajas aquí?Do you work here?
Common Mistake
IncorrectCorrect
You work here?Do you work here?
Why This Happens

This mistake makes sense. Spanish and English organize this idea differently. The goal is not to think “Spanish is wrong,” but to notice where Spanish patterns can interfere with English sentence-building. Once you see the pattern, you can practice the English structure as a whole phrase.

Real English Examples
  • Do you live here?
  • Does she work here?
  • Did they call you?
  • Do we have class?
  • Does he understand?
  • Did she finish?
  • Do you like coffee?
  • Did you see it?
Practice

  3. Build your own sentence using the rule from this chapter.
  4. Choose the correct answer: Do you work here? / You work here?

title: Negatives with Do Not, Does Not, and Did Not
html:
Chapter 4

Negatives with Do Not, Does Not, and Did Not

Sentence Foundations
Big Idea

English often uses do not, does not, and did not to make negative sentences.

Simple Rule

Use do not / does not / did not + base verb.

Spanish Comparison

Spanish uses no before the verb. English needs a helper verb in many sentences.

Contrast box

Spanish thinkingNatural English
No entiendo.I do not understand.
Common Mistake
IncorrectCorrect
I no understand.I do not understand.
Why This Happens

This mistake makes sense. Spanish and English organize this idea differently. The goal is not to think “Spanish is wrong,” but to notice where Spanish patterns can interfere with English sentence-building. Once you see the pattern, you can practice the English structure as a whole phrase.

Real English Examples
  • I do not eat meat.
  • She does not work here.
  • They do not understand.
  • We did not go.
  • He does not like it.
  • I don’t know.
  • She doesn’t agree.
  • We didn’t finish.
Practice
  1. Fix the mistake: I no understand.
  2. Translate into English: No entiendo
  3. Build your own sentence using the rule from this chapter.
  4. Choose the correct answer: I do not understand. / I no understand.
Show answers

  2. Answers may vary, but they should follow the chapter pattern.
  3. Answers may vary.
  4. Choose: I do not understand.

In second language learning, this kind of predictable transfer can be reduced through noticing, contrastive examples, repeated input, and deliberate practice (Swan, 2016).

Quick Review

  • Do not translate word-for-word from Spanish.
  • Practice with short, correct sentences before building longer ones.
  • Use the examples in this chapter as sentence models.

Big Idea

Evidence needs clear signal phrases.

Spanish academic expressions may translate, but English requires agreement and clear verbs.

IncorrectCorrect

Big Idea

Spanish thinkingNatural English

Common Spanish-Speaker Errors
Big Idea

La fluidez viene de la práctica, la retroalimentación y la repetición.

Simple Rule

Usa los patrones de este libro todos los días.

Spanish Comparison

La transferencia desde el español es normal. La meta es notarla y reconstruir los patrones del inglés.

Caja de contraste

Pensamiento en españolInglés natural
Sigo practicando.I can speak clearly with practice.
Common Mistake
IncorrectoCorrecto
I no can speak good.I can speak clearly with practice.
Why This Happens

Este error tiene sentido. El español y el inglés organizan esta idea de forma diferente. La meta no es pensar que "el español está mal", sino notar dónde los patrones del español pueden interferir con la construcción de oraciones en inglés. Cuando ves el patrón, puedes practicar la estructura inglesa como una frase completa.

Real English Examples
  • I practice every day.
  • I learn from mistakes.
  • I speak as much as possible.
  • I review regularly.
  • I listen carefully.
  • I improve slowly.
  • I stay consistent.
  • I keep learning.
Practice
  1. Corrige el error: I no can speak good.
  2. Traduce al inglés: Sigo practicando
  3. Construye tu propia oración usando la regla de este capítulo.
  4. Elige la respuesta correcta: I can speak clearly with practice. / I no can speak good.
Show answers
  1. I can speak clearly with practice.
  2. Las respuestas pueden variar, pero deben seguir el patrón del capítulo.
  3. Las respuestas pueden variar.
  4. Elige: I can speak clearly with practice.
Teacher / Academic Note

Este capítulo trata sobre práctica deliberada, una zona común donde los aprendices hispanohablantes pueden transferir patrones del español al inglés. En el aprendizaje de segundas lenguas, este tipo de transferencia previsible se reduce notando los patrones, comparando ejemplos contrastivos, recibiendo entrada repetida y haciendo práctica deliberada (Krashen, 1985; Swain, 1985).

Quick Review
  • Aprende el patrón inglés como una estructura completa.
  • No traduzcas palabra por palabra desde el español.
  • Practica con oraciones cortas y correctas antes de hacer oraciones largas.
  • Usa los ejemplos de este capítulo como modelos de oración.
Sources and Further Reading
  • Krashen, 1985; Swain, 1985

Chapter 60

Final Review and Next Steps

Common Spanish-Speaker Errors
Big Idea

La fluidité naît de la pratique, du retour et de la répétition.

Simple Rule

Utilisez les schémas de ce livre tous les jours.

Spanish Comparison

Le transfert depuis l'espagnol est normal. L'objectif est de le repérer et de reconstruire les schémas anglais.

Encadré de contraste

Pensée espagnoleAnglais naturel
Sigo practicando.I can speak clearly with practice.
Common Mistake
IncorrectCorrect
I no can speak good.I can speak clearly with practice.
Why This Happens

Cette erreur se comprend. L'espagnol et l'anglais organisent cette idée différemment. L'objectif n'est pas de penser que « l'espagnol se trompe », mais de remarquer où les schémas espagnols peuvent interférer avec la construction de phrases en anglais. Une fois le schéma identifié, on peut pratiquer la structure anglaise comme une expression complète.

Real English Examples
  • I practice every day.
  • I learn from mistakes.
  • I speak as much as possible.
  • I review regularly.
  • I listen carefully.
  • I improve slowly.
  • I stay consistent.
  • I keep learning.
Practice
  1. Corrigez l'erreur : I no can speak good.
  2. Traduisez en anglais : Sigo practicando
  3. Construisez votre propre phrase en utilisant la règle de ce chapitre.
  4. Choisissez la bonne réponse : I can speak clearly with practice. / I no can speak good.
Show answers
  1. I can speak clearly with practice.
  2. Les réponses peuvent varier, mais elles doivent suivre le schéma du chapitre.
  3. Les réponses peuvent varier.
  4. Choisissez : I can speak clearly with practice.
Teacher / Academic Note

Ce chapitre traite de pratique délibérée, un domaine fréquent où les apprenants hispanophones peuvent transférer des schémas de l'espagnol vers l'anglais. En acquisition d'une seconde langue, ce type de transfert prévisible se réduit par la prise de conscience, les exemples contrastifs, l'exposition répétée et la pratique délibérée (Krashen, 1985; Swain, 1985).

Quick Review
  • Apprenez le schéma anglais comme une structure complète.
  • Ne traduisez pas mot à mot depuis l'espagnol.
  • Pratiquez avec des phrases courtes et correctes avant d'en construire de plus longues.
  • Servez-vous des exemples de ce chapitre comme modèles de phrase.
Sources and Further Reading
  • Krashen, 1985; Swain, 1985
